metadata.title: Carmell v. Texas, 529 U.S. 513 (2000) (No. 98-7540)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Carmell v. Texas

Opinion filed: 2000-05-01

Docket No.: 98-7540

Citations:
• 146 L. Ed. 2d 577
• 120 S. Ct. 1620
• 529 U.S. 513
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 3004

Case holding summaries:
• convictions for offenses committed before effective date of amended article 38.07—allowing conviction for certain sexual offenses on uncorroborated testimony of child victim—violated the prohibition against ex post facto laws because convictions rested on uncorroborated testimony
• stating that where the Supreme Court expressly overruled two cases in a decision, it should not be assumed that it impliedly overruled a third in the same decision
• concluding that an elimination of a corroboration requirement went to the “sufficiency of the evidence . . . for meeting the burden of proof” and thus was not a “mode[] of procedure”
• "Sufficiency of the evidence rules (by definition) do just that — they inform us whether the evidence introduced is sufficient to convict as a matter of law [.]"
• Supreme Court has “repeatedly endorsed” Justice Chase’s formulation
• explaining the a plea bargain at that time, no plea discussions took place on distinction
• reaffirming validity of Calder's fourth ex post facto category
• noting changes lowering quantum of proof, and thus implicating Ex Post Facto Clause, will always inure to State's benefit, but witness competency laws "do not necessarily run in the State's favor"
• discussing Calder v. Bull and the common-law under- standing of the term
• stating that "clearly established Federal law" as used in the AEDPA "refers to the holdings, as opposed to the dicta, of [the Supreme Court's] decisions as of the time of the relevant state-court decision "
• Supreme Court has “repeatedly endorsed” Justice Chase’s formulation
• holding that the Ex Post Facto Clause of the U.S. Constitution precluded application of a statute to offenses committed before its effective date
• noting that Collins "eliminated a doctrinal hitch that had developed in our cases, which purported to define the scope of the Clause along an axis distinguishing between laws involving `substantial protections' and those that are merely `procedural.'"
• discussing and applying the fourth definition of an ex post facto law
• to be published at 529 U.S. 513
• discussing and applying the fourth definition of an ex post facto law
• change in rule of evidence that decreased burden on government to prove crime violated the Ex Post Facto Clause when applied to a defendant's case retrospectively
• "[F]or what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly."
• examining the historical circumstances of the case of Sir John Fenwick, cited by Justice Chase as an example of the fourth ex post facto category, in order "[t]o better understand the type of law that falls within that category"
• Wooddeson's categories "correlate precisely to Calder 's four categories"
